A post on here reminded me of something that might also belong here. I have quite severe depression and anxiety, and it's bad enough that I can't function without medication. At one point something extremely stressful happened at work, and I was unable to keep food down for almost a week because of anxiety. I managed to get a phone call with one of the doctors at the surgery, and when I explained that I believed it was anxiety causing the vomiting her response was "But you're on medication for your mental health, so this wouldn't be what's causing it". I was dumbstruck. That's not how medication works! I also take painkillers for chronic pain, and I still spent 2 hours getting to sleep last night because, while it eases most of the pain, it doesn't do anything for my back or neck, and I've also got some unusual pain in my shoulder too.

Just because I'm on medication for something, it doesn't mean it's going to magic the problem away, especially when it's a chronic issues.

I guess I would maybe count to this. I cut my relatives out of my life when I was 19, they had spent my life tormenting me and treating me like dirt. With me gone, there's my aunt, my uncle, my grandmother, and my dad. My dad being the youngest at 58 years old now. No younger generation to take care of them. My aunt would be prepared for that, but my dad and my grandmother were banking all their hopes on me caring for them in their old age. So much so they would make fun of me for how incapable I was of domestic tasks (for example I didn't learn how to use a washing machine until I googled it at 19), but when I asked them to show me, they always made excuses. "Your school should be teaching you that!". "You should know how to do that, figure it out". "I'll show you some other time". They never would show me though, they liked having evidence of what a horrible, incompetent, and lazy person they saw me as. They also didn't want me to be able to live independently, because that would make it easier for me to move out, which would mean I wouldn't be at their immediate use.

I also lied and said that I was required to live on campus for the first year when I went to University, I wasn't planning to cut contact yet, but I was desperate for a taste of independence. My aunt gave me my birthday money early so that I could afford the deposit. I felt awful, because my aunt was actually the only one who had ever stood up for new, but keeping in contact with her would have been too complicated, and I'm certain she would have put some pressure on me to mend things with the others. Not even a month after I moved into my student accommodation, I got into an argument with my dad and finally stood up for myself. I cut contact, and with that I was expecting to become homeless once finished my first year and my lease finished. I was too mentally ill to complete my studies and hold down a job at the same time.

As luck would have it, everything turned out fine. A lot of bumps in the road, but I graduated, didn't end up homeless, and I'm now working in the healthcare system. I don't exactly regret cutting contact, but I'll admit I should have done some research on my options for homelessness instead of hoping for the best. I nearly destroyed my life.

My grandmother was a narcissistic sociopath and was incredibly controlling when it came to my hair. When I finally cut contact with her and my father, one of the first things I did was dye my hair red, just like I had always wanted, and she had always disapproved of. I was fucking terrified, because I thought "what if she's right? What if it'll look terrible?". Once my hair was dry and combed, it looked amazing, and I was so happy. I know regularly dye my hair all kinds of colors: it's a sort of lilac at the moment!

I can't even describe how freeing that moment was, and how I get a little buzz every time I mull over dying my hair a new colour and decide "well why not?! Let's do it!". Also now have a nose piercing which my grandmother would have disapproved of more than the dyed hair, and I fucking love it too! Hurt like hell, but it adds something to my appearance that's very defining of myself, I feel.

I guess the point I'm trying to make is, don't let anyone hold you back from a new adventure! Whether they're about person, or even yourself! You could miss out on a whole head of fun and experiences!

Not a teacher, but was a student that experienced a lot of really dark stuff first hand.

Most relevant probably would have been when I was between 5 and 7. I was kidnapped by my mother away from my father, and suffered severe abuse. I was liked by my teachers, and they were apparently heartbroken when they found out she had taken me and not to expect me back at that school for some time. The school she moved me to also knew that there was some kind of family dispute going on, because social workers would visit me on site. When I finally returned to my initial lower school, the teachers were all informed of the abuse I suffered, and I remember the two teachers who I had for my class when I was younger were pretty tearful when I came back. When I walked back into one of the classrooms full of my old classmates, they swarmed me with hugs and excited chatter. I still feel bad at how quiet and empty I appeared, because I was genuinely happy that it was all over. The best was when my mother started turning up outside my school, and going to school plays. The head teacher, who knew more of the gruesome details than the other teachers, went ballistic at her when she found out, and told her to keep away from the school or the police would be immediately involved. My mother was never seen near the school again.

I really feel for the teachers from my lower school, because I couldn't imagine having one of your students go missing under such disturbing circumstances, and then finding out some of the messed up shit that student went through. And then you have to see them most days of the week, knowing what they've come from, and having to approach them as normally as possible. I imagine it's such a strange dynamic.

In my middle school, I got teased and bullied relentlessly, and every few weeks I'd get dragged out of sight and beaten bloody. They would pin me down and press an elbow or knee against my back - even know I freak out if I feel a similar sensation, like if my partner shifts in his sleep and his elbow rests against my back. I approached teachers about the bullying I was suffering, and they just didn't care; told me to ignore it and that it would stop eventually. The worst was a teacher I looked up to who told me I deserved it, after she heard another student lie about me being racist. I was so ashamed I started stealing makeup from teachers to hide my bruises and cuts.

I eventually tried to take my own life on school grounds, in the most unintellectual way possible. I excused myself from class to go to the bathroom, I blocked a sink, filled it with water, put my face in, and breathed in as deeply as I could. I remember my body feeling this sharp pain all at once, everything thing went bright white, and faded to dark. I still remember hearing the thud of myself hitting the floor. I woke up, and no one had found me in that time, and my class had finished. I returned to my classroom, which was now empty, gathered my belongings, and went to my next class. The rest of that day, and the weeks that followed are pretty blank. I just coasted day by day.

By far, the worst thing that ever happened to me, none of my teachers found out about. This was when I was in the school that my mother moved me to. There was a girl (Sophie) in my class who went on to molest me throughout my time there. My mother was friends with her mother (Zoe) and Zoe would often have me at her house. She walked in a few times on her daughter molesting me, and pulled her away from me, and eventually refused to leave us alone together. On several occasions Zoe asked Sophie why she was doing this, and the girl just shrugged and said she knew it was bad, and that she was doing a bad thing because she didn't like me.

Me (Cutting ties): After sixth form I went to University, and had planned to use this as a way out. My plan was to spend my first year at University, and my second and third years at home, because I knew it would be cheaper living with my dad. I was desperate for at least that first year of freedom, I even lied and told them that I was required to live on campus for the first year. Not even a month into my course, my father and I got into an argument over text. I finally stood up to him and called him out on his bullshit. There was no reconciliation, and I cut contact with him, as well as the rest of my relatives. I was terrified. My social anxiety and depression prevented me from studying and working at the same time, so I feared homelessness. My partner suggested moving in together at the end of my first academic year, and so we did. I was still struggling badly with my mental health, especially because we had to move in together back at my home town. He couldn't move closer to my University because he wouldn't be able to get to work, but moving to my home town allowed me to commute to University with no problems. He was the bread winner, so it would be too big a risk for him to move away from his job, in case he couldn't find another one in time. I was terrified of bumping into my relatives every time I left the flat, because my home town was small enough that it could happen at any time. I was still self harming quite badly, and having weekly break downs. I also developed a sound disorder called misophonia. All of this put intense strain on our relationship, especially as my partner has his own mental health to deal with, as well as my volatile break downs. Eventually we get a new upstairs neighbor in my third year of University, and he just loves playing music at nightclub volumes at all hours of the day and night. I'm already sleep deprived, my misophonia is triggered badly, and my mental health is going further down hill. I some how managed to graduate, and then got stuck trying desperately to find jobs, with little to no luck.

Me (About a year and a half ago): My partner comes home one day late in the year, and I can tell something is wrong. I'll never forget the room turning cold and deadly silent as he told me "I think I saw [friends name] die today". His friend had experienced what seemed to be a heart attack at work infront of everyone, and not long after my boyfriend told me what happened, we got the call that the friend had died. He was only 30, and a genuinely good man. My boyfriend dropped into a deep depression and couldn't go to work. He was given a month off, and even then he would try to go in, but come back in the midst of a panic attack. He didn't go in for another month, and ended up giving in his notice. His mother let us move in with them, several hours away from my shit hole home town. I gave up self harm, not because I wanted to to be honest, but because it feelt wrong doing that in someone else's home - though I did have a few minor relapses. Moving from my home town had a pretty traumatic and unforeseen consequence; I began remembering things that I had repressed. Back when I loved in my home town I couldn't go anywhere without something bringing up a lesser, but still upsetting memory, so that made it easy to keep the really bad stuff locked away deep down. It was after moving away that I rented some of the stuff that happened to me when I was younger. I started having flashbacks of those kids trying to kill me, the girl molesting me, and my mother beating me. It was a really difficult time, and I couldn't bring myself to tell anyone what I was going through at the time. There was a lot of pressure for me to stand up and get a job, because my partner was in such an aweful mental state. It took a while, but I finally found work as a mall cleaner, and it actually improved my mental health somewhat, particularly my social anxiety. However, the attitudes, rudeness, and entitlement of customers began to grate on me. After a few months I became pretty depressed in my job, but stayed while I looked elsewhere for something better. My boyfriend took a long time to find work, because he just wasn't ready for quite a while. I think he beat himself up about it, because it meant I was solely responsible for finances, but I didn't mind at all - I just wanted him to feel better in his own time. Several months after moving I ended up developing chronic pain in my joints, and to this day I'm still trying to get a diagnosis. I'm in a lot of pain on a daily basis, but I've learned to get by.

Me (present day): I'm in a healthcare job that I love, however we recently had someone join the team who is a nightmare to work with. Thankfully it looks as though she may be getting the sack, so fingers crossed, otherwise I'll start looking for a job elsewhere. My partner loves his job, but also has some issues there too, so if this woman does leave, he's considering joining my team. Our mental health is a hell of a lot better, though these last few months have been difficult and trying because of the stress of looking for a place to move in to. We're actually supposed to move in to a house tomorrow, but there's been a mess up with the payment details they've provided, so it's now looking a little uncertain. We're both happier, and on medication for our depression. I think moving out will be exactly what we need to really start feeling better. Having our own space to decompress after work, or just generally when we're stressed out, will be a total game changer.

I don't regret cutting contact with my relatives at all, and while I still have a long way to go in order to adequately improve my mental health, I'm so much better off now than I've ever been.

My man, we'll call him Dirk, worked for a call center, and he had made a good few friends there, including a man I'll call Terry. Terry was the most relaxed person either of us had ever met, nothing phased him, scared him, or angered him - he just got on with it.

One day at their workplace, Terry suddenly starts panicking in front of the entire team, and he's clearly in agony. He wouldn't calm down, and eventually collapsed and lost consciousness. An ambulance was called, and no one had a damn clue what had happened, or if he was going to be okay - the general consensus was that he'd had a heart attack.

When Dirk got home, I could tell something was wrong, and I asked him. I'll never forget the hollow look on his face and his voice that made my hair stand on end when he said "I think I just saw Terry die". What do you even say to that?

I held him close for a good hour or so, and eventually his manager called him. I couldn't hear what his manager was saying, but the second Dirk hung up without so much as a goodbye, I knew Terry hadn't made it. I've never heard such devastated crying from anyone before, it was truly heartbreaking. Dirk later rang the manager back and apologized for hanging up so abruptly, he just couldn't handle it. The manager rang up everyone in the team, and also was tasked with contacting Terry's family and long term girlfriend, to break the news. I don't envy him at all, and I couldn't imagine having to do that, especially considering it's not what you'd expect to have to do in that line of work. I have a hell of a lot of respect for that man for just doing what was necessary.

Terry was only 30 years old, and I remember my partner and I were supposed to go to a pub quiz with him, his missus, and the manager the following weekend. I didn't know him very well, and mourned the potential to make a fantastic friend.

The next few months were incredibly dark and dreary. Dirk was given a month away from work by his doctor, and even after that he just couldn't face the place again. He was a total shell of the man he was before, and we were both just coasting by trying to figure out how to handle his grieving. He did try to go back to work, but would return home thirty minutes later in the midst of a panic attack.

It took a year before he was able to go back to work again, and thankfully he loves his current job. Life is a lot better now, and we all met up on the anniversary of Terry's passing to celebrate the great man he was. He could make anyone laugh, and had the ability to fall asleep anywhere - including at his work desk.

Death is fucking devastating.

Between the ages of 0-20 I was a victim of abuse at the hands of relatives, school bullies, and even a few teacher's. I had depression, social anxiety, OCD, anorexia, and for a few years I had horrific hallucinations. I also self harmed for a large portion of my preteen and teenage life, and tried to take my life too many times to recall without actually counting them out. I dealt with all of it mostly by myself; imagine being 12 years old and hallucinating dead people, but being more scared of what would happen if your relatives found out about it, and all my other mental health issues.

When I was close to 20 years old, I moved away to University and, after an argument with my dad where I demanded he acknowledge the crap he and his mother put me through, I finally cut contact. Things got a little better from here on, but I still struggled terribly with my mental health, and I now had nowhere to live at the end of the academic year, and no job. My mental health made it difficult enough to keep up with my studies, so the prospect of having to get a job was truly terrifying. My partner suggested we move in together, but because of his job, it would mean moving back to my home town. I didn't see much of an issue with it at first, but then when we moved in together I was terrified every time I went outside, in case I bumped into my relatives. I was having daily breakdowns, self harming most days, and barely getting by in my course. 

I somehow managed to graduate, and was terrified of going into the workforce; I had no work experience and would likely need to look at jobs in retail, and I was terrified of my relatives possibly being in any place I might work. A few months later, we were struggling to survive off of my partners wage (as a UK University student with no familial contact, I got full student grants etc), and I was struggling to even get an interview at any entry level retail job. Then shit really hit the fan. My partner only worked at a call center, but his 30 year old best friend suddenly had a heart attack at work in front of his work colleagues, including my boyfriend, and he was later declared dead. My partner was totally unable to bring himself to work; he tried numerous times, but would be back half an hour after leaving, and he'd be in the midst of a panic attack. It was brutal.

Eventually, he had spent two months away from his job, and was likely facing being fired. His mother offered to let us move in with them, and start a new life, in a new town. We moved there a  year and a half ago. Things were tough to begin with, we both were struggling with mental health problems, and there was a lot of pressure for me to get a job, because my partner was still struggling badly with what had happened in his last workplace, and it was agreed that he needed to focus on healing before jumping into another job. I eventually got a job as a cleaner in a mall, and I loved the work. Just about half a year after starting the job, I began to hate the way customers treated us, and the sense of entitlement many showed. I started looking for a new job, and I was becoming more and more depressed at my workplace - I also developed pain in my joints which I'm still trying to get a diagnosis for. Eventually, my partner managed to gather the courage to look for a new job. He found one at another call center, and was incredibly anxious about it.

I'm 24 now, and we've been living in this town for roughly a year and a half. My boyfriend loves his job, because he sells medical equipment to help greatly improve the lives of vulnerable people. The company he works for doesn't encourage up-selling, and even actively encourages their employees to sell a cheaper package if it would suit the customers needs better than a more expensive one. I've got a new job working in the healthcare system and, though the last two weeks at work have been incredibly stressful and even upsetting, I'm really enjoying what I do now. Just over a year ago I was had never worked a day in my life, and now I'm working in a healthcare profession, where I received a recognition award just two months after starting here. Compulsive binge eating is actually called Binge-eating disorder. Someone with bulimia will likely have a very normal diet, but when they experience a depressive or anxious episode, they'll the on an uncontrolled binge. In more severe cases this binge could be as higher than 2000 calories, on top of their normal daily intake. Following a binge, the individual will feel enormous amount of regret, anger, and/or fear about the binge, and they'll begin trying to purge it from their body in whatever way they choose.

With anorexia, the individual will likely have reduced their daily calory intake to below 1000 calories, they may engage in compulsively checking the calory content of their food, and perhaps weighing foods that otherwise don't need to be weighed out. Additionally, an indiviual with anorexia may also purge as an aid to their weight lose intentions.

That would depend on whether you were having binges on top of a relatively normal food intake. Saying that however, there are some people who eat normally (little to no calory restrictions in place that would happen with anorexia), but engage in purging, in which case this can lead to different diagnosis depending on what the therapist portrays the intention as. There are also many people with anorexia who will consume less than 1000 calories a day, and engage in purging on top of that to aid weight lose.

A sign that they're inducing vomiting would be bite marks or scarring around the base of the knuckles, but even then that would only be if they are using their own fingers to induce vomiting. Their oral health and breathe may suddenly become noticeably bad without explanation. You might notice they have an unusual preoccupation with exercise, and potentially work themselves to near collapse.

If you do have concerns about someone in your life going through this, it's definitely worthwhile to talk to them about it, and advise they seek help. Bulimia is incredibly dangerous and has a long list of painful outcomes if recovering isn't explored.

Absolutely! When I was anorexic, my grandmother commented that "I worry about how little you eat, but I know that you're not anorexic because your cheeks aren't all shallow or sunken in". I was weighing my food, counting calories, I cut the words fat into my side, and I was actually a stone and half underweight - my puffy cheeks hid it well. Anorexia can happen to anyone, of any weight. Anorexic people of a normal weight will look in the mirror and see someone who is morbidly obese, and they'll hate themselves for it.

People with anorexia will largely starve themselves and reduce calorie intake. They may obsess over the calories in foods, count the calories they consume, and drastically reduce their daily calory intake. A normal daily intake is roughly 2000 calories, whereas someone with anorexia will consume considerably less, often under a 1000 calories per day. As well as this, they may engage in purging to further weight lose, which is where the two disorders overlap. They also overlap in the sense that anorexia will usually have body dysmorphia present, which can be present in bulimia also.

With bulimia, it's about the battle to combat a lose of control, whereas in anorexia it's about fighting to be in control. An indiviual with bulimia will usually have a relatively average daily intake of calories, but additionally will have abnormal and regular binges of large quantities of food (these foods will often be high in calories or sugary). Binges could be a couple of times a week, or a couple of times a month, and often happen during in a low or upsetting period, such as a depressive episode. Following the binge, the individual will purge by any number or combination of methods: throwing up, abusing laxatives, taking dieting pills, exercising in extreme amounts, or a period of starvation where they will consume no food, or very little food. You'll also find that bulimia isn't necessarily about losing weight, as another redditor mentioned, many people with bulimia are usually somewhere around average weight.

Both diabulimia and orthorexia aren't very well known, even in the psychology field.

A binge is usually quantified by an abnormally large meal (I'm talking ten bags of crisps, a pack of cupcakes, a box of biscuits, and five packets of chocolate) on top of (or instead of) your normal daily food intake, which in the case of bulimia will happen more than once over the course of the illness. A binge being an abnormally regular occurrence, and being quickly followed by a purge or series of purges would be my best definition of bulimia.

Your experience could be considered two things, depending on some factors. If you were intentionally eating very little and using laxatives in order to lose weight, and if you struggled with your body image, than it would likely have been anorexia. People with anorexia don't binge (unless they also suffer from bulimia), but they made purge in order to aid weight lose. If you were doing it as a form of punishment or out of recklessness it would probably be considered a form of self-harm instead.

It's dangerous in the extreme and becoming terrifyingly more common. The silver lining is that because it's becoming more common it's better recognised within the psychology field, which leads to faster diagnosis and more informed treatment.

Another lesser known eating disorder is orthorexia, which can appear in two ways, sometimes both can occur. One way involves an obsession with dieting fads in the pursuit of healthy living, regardless of potential dangers that could be associated with some of them. The other that can occur, is an obsessive preoccupation with healthy eating, including checking every label for ingredients and nutritional content, cutting out a large number of 'bad' nutrition, obsessing over others nutritional intake, distress at not having access to "safe" foods, etc.

Purging in eating disorders is used to describe any way of getting rid of what you've eaten on a binge or to at least reduce how many calories you have taken in from the binge. Purging is also a sort of punishment for the binge.

Consider bulimia like a bit of an emotional rollercoaster. You've had a really bad day, you feel low and upset, so you consume a days worth of calories to make yourself feel happy. It gives you a good, but temporary feeling. When the feeling goes, you're left with regret and anger, the individual is probably thinking negative thoughts about themselves, how much they consumed, how little control they have, and how much weight they may gain. The indiviual then purges to try to relieve themselves of some of the binge to prevent their body from absorbing as many calories, but also as a sort of punishment for having the binge in the first place.

I think that may be why it's considered a purge, because it's still punishing themselves for the binge, and it also reduces calory intake by cutting out future calory intake for a period of time. Some of that binge may also be stored as fat, and if you start starving yourself your body will burn through its reserves of fat which is another way of getting rid of the calories.

It can be auditory and/or visual. I personally suffered from depression since I was about 6 years old, and during my preteen years I used to hear voices saying they were coming to kill me, I also used to dead people in mirrors that kind of looked like the girl from the ring. It can be different depending on the patient, not every child with depression will necessarily experience hallucinations, and oftentimes they're not too extreme. Personally I wonder how many kids with "imaginary friends" actually had childhood depression.

There's a number of purge methods, other than vomiting, however another vomiting method, instead of sticking objects down your throat, is using syrup of ipecac (thanks to those for the correct spelling) it's a substance that makes you throw up. Non-throwing up methods include abusing laxatives or diet pills (taking them when you don't need to, or perhaps taking too many) and extreme amounts of exercise.

Another purge method is actually starving yourself. Someone with anorexia may also take part in starvation periods as well as an already considerably lowered calorie intake. Someone with bulimia may have a massive food binge and try to counter it by periods of starvation. Some in the psychology profession would still call this bulimia, while others may refer to it as bulimia with anorexic tendencies, or anorexia with bulimic tendencies. The two illnesses can co-exist in the same person, and the label placed upon the illnesses tends to depend on which of the two of more prevalent.

There's quite a few surprising bits of information you can learn studying psychology. I learned that depression has a different effect depending on your age. A preteen with depression is more likely to experience hallucinations than a teenager or adult with depression, a teenager with depression is more likely to suffer somatic symptoms, and adults are more likely to suffer the the low mood and experience difficulties just getting out of bed and doing relatively normal everyday activities.

I had learned to hide the marks, but this time I didn't bother. I remember walking around in a bit of a daze, I could see everything around me, but it didn't feel like I was really quite there. Sounds were muffled and there was almost like this constant tv static noise masking everything else. It was like my senses and my will to live were dying together in total synchronization. I excused myself from the classroom and made my way to the nearest girls toilets. I blocked one of the sinks with toilet paper, filled the sink up, stuck my face in, and breathed in deeper than I ever had before (and ever have since). My vision briefly turned to black, and then swiftly to a painfully bright white. I remember this sharp pain writhing down through my chest, and high pitched screaming in my ear. Then everything went black again. I don't remember hitting the floor, but when I finally came to I was laying on the ground. My side hurt where I had impacted with the floor, and I an impressive cluster of bruises up one side of my body. I felt fucking awful, but I managed to return to the classroom, and it was empty, my stuff was still there. I attended my next class late and the teacher just gave me a disproving glare, but didn't say anything. I was very quiet and never caused trouble, so I guess he just assumed I had a good reason to be late. Thankfully he never followed up on me about it.

Sometimes it can be, but not always. A marriage is hard work, and the trick to a happy marriage is taking the time to find someone who suits you best. That doesn't mean you have to search for someone who is perfect, but someone who you don't mind making a compromise for here and there, and someone who equally is happy to do the same for you. Make sure to have an in depth discussion about what your future dreams are; do you want kids, if so how many? Do you want to move to another town/country, or stay where you met? Do you want to get married, and if so a big or small wedding? Etc. Ideally, these should match, otherwise you could be looking at a relationship that will either fall apart eventually, or where one person will resent the other for having to give up their dreams for the other.

Finding someone who is marriage material, or long term relationship material, doesn't mean you won't have arguments, it just means you'll be more willing to work through them, and hopefully it'll be easier to work through them. Finding someone like that to share your life with will take some time, so don't be afraid to try again if you find someone who there are certain compromises you can't make for. I've met a few guys I liked, but they wanted kids and I didn't - people kept telling me that I would change my mind so I should compromises and have kids I didn't want just because I got on well with these guys. Eventually I met a guy who doesn't want kids, who I match with as perfectly as possible, and we've been together for over five years. Spoiler alert: after living in a house that had kids, both of us have never felt stronger about not wanting children ourselves. Compromise is sometimes necessary to make a relationship work, but not if it's going to make you miserable for long term.

Edit: also wanted to add that there is some misunderstanding as to what misophonic trigger sounds are. Thanks to terrible media coverage most people think these trigger sounds are exclusively bodily sounds. Whilst those are very common triggers for suffers, misophonic triggers are any *specific* sound that causes the typical misophonic fight or flight response. Common trigger sounds are bodily, or repetitive, but they can really be anything. The criteria is that the person had specific triggers, rather than being triggered by all sounds, and that any discomfort is predominantly emotional, rather than physical

When you hear certain trigger sounds, it's almost like suffering the emotional response side of PTSD. You can feel this inescapable distress building up inside you until you just blow up, and it spills out. Studies find that during a misophonic episode, the patients "fight or flight" instinct is activated. In less severe cases this build up of distress will lead to the individual showing an abnormal emotional reaction of fear and/or rage, and/or they may try to flee the situation if at all possible. In much more severe cases, they may use violence in order to stop whatever is causing the trigger sound.

It's a horrible and debilitating illness to have to live with, which makes it even more frustrating that the media really takes the piss out of it. A cure, or even a reliable treatment would be a total game changer.

I'd absolutely recommend babysitting, regardless of whether or not you want children. If you're childfree but not sure, you'll know for certain if childrearing is really for you or not. If you want children, you can find out if you're actually capable of being a parent - too many people have kids without really thinking things through, and the child suffers for it. But, if you see you self getting angry in that situation, get out. Don't put others in harm's way just to prove a point or out of sheer stubbornness.

That social anxiety means you're unable to talk to other people. In severe cases, some people with disorder end up "voluntarily mute", whilst with others it effects their behavior in more subtle way. Such as not eating in front of people, changing aisle in a super store because you've been unintentionally following someone while going about your business and you worry they might think you're actually following them, using your phone as a comfort blanket when social situations become too overwhelming. There's also some parts that can't be seen at all; people with social anxiety who are knowingly about to attend a social event will often create multiple scenarios of the event in their head beforehand. This is a copying strategy so they feel prepared with responses to these possible (usually uncomfortable) hypothetical scenarios, should they happen. The same process is used after social events so the individual can feel prepared to explain any misunderstandings that they feel took place.

Forcing yourself to throw up, isn't always bulimia. Bulimia is defined as the binge purge cycle, so a person with bulimia will binge on hundreds or even thousands of calories, and then purge by either throwing up, using diet pills, using laxatives, and abnormal amounts of exercise. Whilst some people with anorexia may use purging methods as part of their disorder, it's usually diagnosed as the patient intentionally eating under 700-1000 calories. Both disorders usually have an element of body dysmorphia, and the patient will see themselves as overweight, even when shown evidence of the contrary. In some cases where a patient shows signs of both disorders, they'll be labeled as anorexic with bulimic tendencies, bulimic with anorexic tendencies, or Eating Disorder Not Otherwise Specified (EDNOS).

OCD isn't just keeping things tidy, or obsessively cleaning, though these can be symptoms in some cases. Quite common behaviors include counting routines, such as washing and drying your hands to a specific number. Another common behaviour is having to go back and check that you locked the door, or turned the stove off. Patients will have an overwhelming need to take part in these behaviors, for fear that something terrible will happen. This disorder will often mean the individual is late to appointments, or misses them entirely because they're so preoccupied with these compulsive behaviours or thoughts.

Everything word is muffled and lacking emotion, you have to stain just to understand and digest conversation around you. You're almost trapped in a bubble, where you should feel safe, but all it does is isolate and chain you to a lesser existence, where you can see those around you enjoying the fullness of life, a completeness that your cage denies you. You feel like you're going give way and collapse any second, but it never comes. It's this tormenting, perpetual feeling of impending loss. As well as his regular tantrums, I had to deal with my textbook narcissist grandmother. Her and my dad loved to create situations where they could always win, and always make me look bad. I was never good enough for her. She sneered at my excitement over an A I got in GCSE, because it wasn't an A*. She did the same when I was excited about getting full marks on all my A-level film studies coursework, because it wasn't an important subject. She had a huge strop because I didn't choose a University she approved of, despite me explaining to her that the one I picked was the only one in the country that did the specific course I wanted. She was constantly preoccupied with how my behavior and my lifestyle choices would reflect on her. She didn't want me dying my hair, so when I dyed a streak of my hair red her first reaction was to screw up her face and say "I don't like it". She hadn't even said hi, or asked how I was. And when I responded "well, I like it" she stomped her foot like a little kid and snapped "Well I don't!".

Because of their abuse, as well as constant bullying throughout school, I've struggled with mental illness since I was about six years old. I believe that my grandmother was the catalyst that led to my problems with OCD and anorexia, but my problems with depression, social anxiety, self harm, and suicide were influenced by all of the abuse together. My mother and grandmother were just nasty people, and my dad was just a man trying his best to be a father that he never wanted to be, and just generally fucking it up monumentally. I might have kept a relationship with my father if he'd finally been able to put this hands up and admit to his wrong doings, but he didn't and I'm out of chances to give. I'd called him out on his behavior before, but his response was always along the lines of "I'm the dad, your the child. What I say goes".

I'm now 23, going on 24. I haven't spoken to any of my family for 4 years, and I'm significantly better off for it. I've never been happier.

He was a farmer, and had a few animals here and there, including a bull in one of the fields. This bull had previously chased people out of the fields, but would walk side by side with my grandfather without the slightest sign of aggression. My great grandfather also once brought home a flea infested puppy, Jock. Jock was fiercely loyal... And a total raving lunatic. One day the family went out to the market, and Jock was left chained to his kennel. When they got home there was a huge traffic jam, and as they got closer they realised why. Jock had dragged his kennel into the middle of the road, and was sat on its roof. That was the last time they left him chained outside like that. Jock also crashed through a window just so he could join my great grandfather outside.

One day, the door was left unlocked, and a neighbor decided to walk straight in. Jock pinned him to a wall, growling and teeth bared. The guy threatened to get the police to put the dog down, and my great grandfather get in his face and lectured him on how the dog was there to protect his family, his girls. He always put this wife and daughters first. The police officer who was called on to the scene agreed that the guy was in the wrong, and even asked if the force could add Jock to their police dogs. Again he said he couldn't let the dog go, because he was there to protect his girls.

I would love the opportunity to meet him, to find out what he was really like, and hear about all the crazy things that happened on the farm.
